idiom_name: visitor class hierarchy with a runtime capability check (instanceof or brand), defaults by inheritance
implementation_notes: TypeScript can type the classic structure but cannot supply its runtime half: interfaces are erased, so the extended visitor must be detectable through a class (`processor instanceof UnionProcessor`) or an explicit brand property, because a structural test ('forUnion' in processor) accepts any object that happens to have the member. Adding an element kind means adding the element class, an interface that extends the visitor interface with the new method and, for each operation that wants to handle it, a subclass of the existing visitor that inherits its behaviour and implements the new member; recursion inside the base class then has to go through a virtual factory (`protected make(...)`) or the derived case is lost on nested nodes. When the element set is closed, the idiomatic TypeScript is a discriminated union plus a switch whose default branch calls an assertNever helper, which the compiler checks via the never type - and that is the roadmap that retires the visitor.
pitfalls: An interface is erased at runtime: the capability check must target a class or a brand, and a structural test accepts any object that happens to expose the member, so accidental implementations pass silently.

Only discriminated unions get exhaustiveness checking (via a never-typed default branch); an interface- or class-based visitor has no such guarantee, so an unhandled element kind reaches the default path at runtime.
Extending an operation by subclassing creates a parallel class hierarchy: base-class recursion must go through a virtual factory, otherwise nested nodes are processed by the base implementation only.

Structural typing makes the extended visitor interface satisfiable by unrelated classes, so a visitor compiled against a different but identically shaped hierarchy type-checks and then misbehaves at runtime.
